note: Dante names the game: zara, played with three dice, the players calling out the number they bet on. It was a common street game in his Italy.

The winner of the dice game. As he walks off, the bystanders crowd him for a share of his winnings, and he gets free by handing something to each. Dante is the winner here: what the souls want from him is prayer.

These are the souls of Canto 5, who died by violence and repented at the last moment. Each asks Dante to tell the living to pray for them, since prayers from earth shorten the wait below the gate of Purgatory.
Benincasa da Laterina, a judge. He had sentenced a relative of Ghino di Tacco to death, and Ghino took revenge by killing him as he sat in court in Rome.
Ghino di Tacco, a Sienese nobleman turned highwayman, the most famous bandit of his day. Boccaccio later made him the hero of a story in the Decameron.

Usually identified as Guccio de' Tarlati, of a leading Ghibelline family of Arezzo, who drowned in the Arno. Dante's phrase can mean either that he was chasing his enemies or that they were chasing him, and the early commentators disagree.
Federigo Novello, of the Conti Guidi, the great lords of the upper Arno valley. He was killed around 1290 in fighting with the Bostoli family of Arezzo.
The son of Marzucco degli Scornigiani, murdered in the faction fights of Pisa in the 1280s. Early commentators give his name as Gano or Farinata.
A Pisan nobleman who had become a Franciscan friar. When his son was murdered he did not seek revenge but forgave the killers, which in a city of vendettas took more strength than striking back.
Orso degli Alberti, murdered by his cousin in 1286. The feud began with their fathers, two brothers who killed each other and lie frozen together in the ice of Inferno 32.
Chamberlain and favorite of King Philip III of France, hanged in 1278 on a charge of treason. Dante takes the view that he was innocent, brought down by jealous courtiers and by the queen.

Marie of Brabant, Philip III's second wife, whom Dante blames for Pierre's death. She was still alive in 1300, so the warning is real: repent, or join the "worse flock" of the damned for a false accusation.
The Aeneid, Book 6. In the underworld the drowned helmsman Palinurus begs to be taken across the river, and the Sibyl answers: stop hoping that the decrees of the gods can be bent by prayer.
Virgil's answer: God's justice is not lowered. The debt is still paid in full, but the burning love of the person who prays can pay in a moment what the soul would have paid by long waiting.
Palinurus was a pagan, praying to pagan gods. A prayer made outside God's grace could change nothing.

context: Her first naming on the mountain. Virgil, who is reason, leaves questions of faith to her. Dante will meet her in the garden at the summit (Purgatorio 30), and at her name he suddenly wants to hurry.

note: It is the afternoon of Easter Sunday. The poets are on the eastern slope, and the sun has passed behind the mountain.
The sun. Dante hopes to reach Beatrice today, but the climb will take far longer: he spends three nights on the mountain.
Dante is in the mountain's shade and casts no shadow. Until now his shadow has shown every soul he met that he is alive.
Dante the poet, looking back, speaks to the soul directly. Lombard had a wide sense in his day: a man of northern Italy.

quote: like a lion when it rests
note: A picture of calm strength, not of threat: watchful and dignified, and in no hurry to move.

context: Virgil gets no further than the name of his city. He may be starting the epitaph tradition gave him, which begins "Mantua bore me".
The aloof soul leaps up at one word. He does not yet know this is Virgil: he embraces a stranger simply because they come from the same town.

note: The most famous outburst in the poem. Dante breaks off the story and speaks in his own voice to the end of the canto. The sixth canto of each part is political: Florence in Inferno 6, Italy here, the Empire in Paradiso 6.
Roman law called Italy not a province but the mistress of the provinces. Now, Dante says, she is for sale to anyone.

context: Two dead men from one town embrace at its name, while the living of a single city tear each other apart.
The bridle is the law he put in order. The horse is Italy, and the saddle is empty because no emperor comes to enforce the law. Having good laws and no one to apply them only adds to the shame.

note: The clergy, and above all the popes. Dante held that the Church should keep to spiritual things and leave government to the emperor. By grasping at political power, it has made Italy ungovernable.
The emperor: every Holy Roman Emperor was Caesar's heir. What God teaches is Christ's saying in the Gospels: give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.

context: Emperor-elect at the time of the journey. He should be riding the wild horse of Italy, and has never set foot there.

quote: just judgment fall from the stars
note: A prophecy written after the event. Albert's eldest son died in 1307, and Albert himself was murdered by his nephew in 1308.
Henry VII of Luxembourg, elected in 1308. He did come to Italy, in 1310, and Dante put all his hopes in him. Henry died in 1313 with nothing achieved.

context: Father and son both stayed in Germany, building up their family's lands. Rudolf sits among the negligent rulers in the next canto.

note: Italy, the fairest part of the empire and the seat of Rome, left to run wild.

In Italian, Montecchi and Cappelletti. For Dante they were not two families of one city but two factions: the Montecchi of Verona and the Cappelletti of Cremona, on opposite sides of Lombardy's wars. Later legend made them the feuding houses of Verona, and Shakespeare took the story from there.
Rival families of Orvieto, one Guelph and one Ghibelline, who fought for control of the city.
The county of the Aldobrandeschi family in southern Tuscany, an old fief of the empire. "Secure" is sarcasm: Siena was taking it apart piece by piece. One of the family speaks in Purgatorio 11.
Rome without her emperor, pictured as the Bible pictures fallen Jerusalem in Lamentations: a widow weeping in the night.

quote: how the people love each other
note: Bitter sarcasm.
Christ, called by the name of the king of the Roman gods. Dante sometimes uses Jove as a poetic name for the true God. It is a bold moment: he asks God whether he has looked away.

Probably the Roman consul Marcellus, a fierce opponent of Julius Caesar: every village politician now sets himself up against the emperor. Others think of an earlier Marcellus, a famous general, so that every upstart passes for a hero.

context: Everything from here to the end is irony. Having said that none of this concerns Florence, Dante shows that she is the worst case of all.

note: Others keep justice in their hearts and speak of it with care. The Florentines talk of it constantly, and that is where it stays.
Elsewhere good men have to be pressed into public office. In Florence everyone grabs at it.
The Greek cities famous for their laws, given by Solon in Athens and Lycurgus in Sparta.

Often linked to the autumn of 1301. The city government that took office in October was thrown out in early November, when the Black Guelphs seized Florence. Dante's own exile followed from that coup.
The limbs are the citizens. Each change of regime drove one party into exile and called another home.
